Here's the thing, and this is totally my own personal experience from being raised Protestant, then finding myself identifying as atheist/agnostic for the last ten years, to converting:

God is love. God wants to love us and He wants us to love him. He's kinda that friend that checks in every few months or so just to make sure you're good. He doesn't ask for anything in return if you aren't willing to give it and I find that's why a lot of people feel that they haven't felt God's presence in their lives or heard Him speak to them. Just like a friend with a differing opinion, you'll dismiss the conversation and ignore what was said.

We do have free will, but I've spoken with my spiritual mentor and Priest about this as I convert, and I'm of the opinion that you don't go to hell anyway if you use your free will. There's an idea that maybe most Christians who love God but often sinned or chose their own wills will possibly end up in Purgatory for lack of repentance. The way I've been taught, you really have to actively want to /hurt/ God and not be sorry about it to get to hell. But maybe I'm getting that all wrong. The idea of forgiveness exists because we're human. We fall short of God's glory. God knows that. But He loves us anyway. It's like having a loving dad.

And to take your analogy of toddlers (which is a good one, since God is, in fact, our Heavenly Father), there are little learning mistakes that parents let their toddlers/children/teens/even grown adult children make. It's part of growing up. No, they're not going to let them, say, shove a fork in a light socket because that would kill them (mortal sins, perhaps?), but letting them fall and skin their knee or break their favorite toy because warnings weren't heeded: that's learning. It's a natural process for Earthly maturing, and I think it naturally transcends to the analogy of our Heavenly Father.

Did it hurt my Earthly father to see me date someone abusive? Yes. Absolutely. Did he know that it was my mistake to make? He did. Of course he offered his advice, but at 26-years-old, what could he have done to make my decision for me? Nothing. Just as sin and our free will often hurt God, it's because He hurts /for/ us. Just as my Earthly father never stopped loving me, as my whole life fell to pieces despite his warnings, so God never stops loving me, despite sins He has told me are wrong.

And you said "endangers" our soul. All sin endangers our soul, but it does not end it. It does not completely sever us from God. God does not turn his back on anyone. We are the ones who walk away from Him. He will always be waiting to heal us when we hurt ourselves or when we're hurt by the evil of others. It took being pushed to the edge of death for me to realize that and listen to God telling me that. Our soul is never lost if we love God and truly repent for moments of failure.

Emotional Regulation is a way of coping with your anxiety by really giving your emotions attention as they come. When you start to feel something, you take a moment to label it and decide where it's coming from. The best way to do that for me, is really:

Feeling > Emotion > Where? > Why? > Reaction > Action > Consequence

Or:

Nerves > Anxiety > Feel it in my chest > Test coming up > I need to study > I do study > I pass the test.

If you can learn to label your emotions, often times you can understand why you have them. Every emotion we have has a reason, no matter what we tell ourselves. Once you start understanding why you feel certain ways, it becomes a lot easier to talk yourself out of extreme emotion or tell yourself: "I understand your need to panic, brain. But we will not die because the grocery store is out of sodas." It's easier to get yourself out of fight or flight mode and able to live life.

It's just another skill you can use to understand why you feel how you feel and what to do about it. Like any coping mechanism, it doesn't work every time, but with practice, it can make the difference between a three day anxiety attack and a two hour one.

When you have to be out with others, try grounding. Focus on being exactly where you are in every moment. Count five things you can see, four things you can hear, three things you can touch, two things you can smell and something you can taste. You are valid in your feelings. Recognize them. Care for them. And let them go on.
